items.request: Explain in plain words why character-level modeling needs the whole corpus as one text first: instead of GPT-2 byte-pair tokens, each character becomes an integer, so the script must first have all of Shakespeare as raw text. Name the idea once (character-level tokenization).
items.why: A short definition to read frames what the script produces and why text comes first.

items.request: Show lines 13-17 of data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py: the input path built next to the script with os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), ...) and the download that runs only if os.path.exists is false. Mark the existence check on line 14 and say what a second run does.
items.why: The learner needs to see the actual guard lines to point at the check.

items.request: Small runnable cells: write a short sample text with a few lines, open it with io.StringIO, call read() as the script does on line 20, and print the type, length in characters, and first 30 characters with newline marks. Show the result is one string, not split by line or word. Let the learner edit the text and rerun.
items.why: Trying read() on a tiny text shows the result is one string whose length counts characters.

items.request: The recorded run says the corpus has 1,115,394 characters. Ask which pair of train and validation sizes loses nothing: 1,003,854 and 111,540, or pairs that do not sum to 1,115,394. Feedback shows the addition.
items.why: A quick computation lets the learner check the later split loses nothing.
